summary:
Health Atlas is a bilingual crew health console prototype that helps astronauts understand health changes, maintain daily wellbeing, and recognize when to seek help. Designed for crew members who are not medical professionals, it connects health monitoring, symptom reporting, and medical communication in one interface.

The console combines 13 health indicators, interactive 3D anatomy for reporting symptoms, personal trends, and explainable rule-based alerts. Physical activity tools include a 3D exercise trainer and routine tracking, while mental wellbeing features offer mood check-ins, journaling, guided breathing, cognitive exercises, and an immersive Earth-view “Cupola” experience. An offline, rule-based assistant provides contextual guidance. Structured reports support flight-surgeon review, and an emergency coordination workflow demonstrates symptom sharing, crew notifications, and help acknowledgments.

Drawing on NASA health references, OSDR laboratory reference ranges, and DONKI space-weather information, Health Atlas addresses the challenge by turning separate measurements and activities into a connected, understandable workflow. Its offline-first design explores support for greater crew autonomy when connectivity is limited. The prototype uses simulated crew health data and provides monitoring and decision support—not diagnosis, treatment, or validated fitness-for-duty decisions.
details:
Health Atlas is a bilingual English–Turkish crew health console prototype designed to help astronauts understand their health, maintain daily wellbeing routines, and communicate concerns. Rather than treating monitoring, exercise, mental wellbeing, and medical reporting as separate activities, it brings them into one connected workflow.

Our central design question was: How can a crew member without professional medical training understand what has changed, record what they are experiencing, and recognize when help may be needed?

What It Does and How It Works

Health monitoring and symptom reporting

The dashboard presents eight key indicators, with a broader catalog of 13 covering physiological measurements, sleep, mood, reaction time, exercise, hydration, radiation, and cabin CO₂. Users can explore historical charts, reference information, and explanations of why each indicator matters.

An interactive 3D anatomy model allows users to select body regions and individual muscle or bone structures, then record symptoms and severity. These reports connect to the complaint history, alerts, exercise guidance, and physician-facing information.

A deterministic analysis engine evaluates configured reference bands, deviations from personal baselines, and sustained trends. Alerts explain the values and rules that triggered them. Source-supported references and prototype-specific rules are distinguished rather than presented as equally validated medical criteria.

Physical and mental wellbeing

The physical activity page combines animated 3D exercise demonstrations, routine completion tracking, and a rule-based exercise coach. Recorded complaints inform the prototype’s routine suggestions; these suggestions are not individualized medical prescriptions.

The mental wellbeing page includes mood check-ins, private journaling, guided breathing, cognitive exercises, and an immersive Earth-view “Cupola” experience. These features support reflection and daily wellbeing activities without claiming to diagnose or treat psychological conditions.

Assistance, reporting, and emergency coordination

One contextual assistant serves as a health-information guide, exercise coach, or supportive companion. Its current implementation is offline and rule-based, with contextual actions such as recording a complaint or navigating to relevant information. An optional language-model integration is prepared but is not connected in the submitted prototype.

Users can generate structured health reports for flight-surgeon review. A separate physician view summarizes crew information and incoming messages.

The emergency workflow demonstrates press-and-hold activation, symptom sharing, notification tracking, and acknowledgments from potential helpers. It is an emergency coordination demonstration—not a validated treatment protocol or an operational spacecraft communication system.

NASA Resources and Data Transparency

Health Atlas uses NASA resources for distinct purposes:

  • OSDR provides laboratory reference ranges used in the blood-test demonstration.
  • DONKI supplies space-weather context, separate from personal radiation-dose records.
  • EPIC and SVS provide Earth imagery and visual resources.
  • NASA human-research and technical references inform educational content and selected monitoring rules.

Simulated crew measurements are identified as fictional. Laboratory reference ranges are not presented as validated astronaut-specific alert thresholds. Cached NASA snapshots display retrieval information so users can distinguish stored information from current updates.

Technology and Development

We developed the prototype using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Three.js and React Three Fiber power the interactive anatomy, exercise trainer, and Cupola scenes. A Node.js server provides APIs, a rule-based analysis and simulation engine, and local persistence through SQLite.

The project includes Vitest and Testing Library for unit and component testing, Playwright for end-to-end and visual testing, and axe-based accessibility checks. External services are mocked in tests to avoid dependence on connectivity or private API keys.

Claude Code assisted software development, and Higgsfield was used to generate the opening video. The prototype does not require specialized hardware; sensor integration remains future work.

Creativity, Design Considerations, and Intended Impact

The project’s creative contribution is the connection between spatial symptom reporting, understandable health trends, wellbeing activities, contextual assistance, and medical communication. The anatomy model is not simply decorative: it provides a shared interaction point for recording and reviewing concerns.

We prioritized low cognitive load, offline operation, bilingual access, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion preferences, and status labels that combine text, icons, and color. We also considered source traceability, explainable alerts, and the distinction between personal reflection and information shared with a physician.

Health Atlas aims to demonstrate how a unified console could support more informed crew participation in health management when connectivity or immediate specialist support is limited. It remains a hackathon prototype: clinical validation, operational evaluation, sensor integration, and server-enforced authentication and access control are required before any real-world medical deployment.
